The manuscript “Subsurface Ocean Turbulent Mixing Enhances Central Pacific ENSO as Positive Feedback” by Liu et al
demonstrates the impact of vertical turbulent mixing on sea surface temperature variability in the equatorial Pacific. The
authors use density overturns in quality controlled ARGO profiles to infer mixing events around the entertainment layer. The
authors also assert that there is a more pronounced effect of the mixing feedback on Central Pacific ENSO events (CP)
versus Eastern Pacific (EP) events. The method is innovative and a good use of existing data from Argo to estimate a
quantity that is elusive. There are some questions I believe should be addressed before the manuscript should be fully
considered for publication.
Major comments
The authors rely on the state of marginal stability as given by Richardson number around 0.25 to substitute stratification for
shear in their relationships they employ to estimate Jq. The authors rightly state in the extended section that the assumption
of marginal instability only holds in the presence of strong background currents inducing vertical shear. In this manuscript
this is assumed to be true within 3S-3N around the equator. However, the observed undercurrent which gives rise to the
strong current shear is shown in for example Johnson et al (2002) or Roger (Karnasukas et al 2020) to span at most 2S-2N.
A rigorous analysis of which profiles, at which location are analyzed needs to be presented, and reasonable arguments
need to be made why the marginal stability assumption holds, even away from the strongest current system. Whitt et al (as
referenced in the manuscript) examine 3N partially in relation to strong mixing induced by tropical instability waves, no
mention of TIW kinetic energy is made here. In the introduction of the text the authors reference the number of Argo profiles
5S-5N. These discrepancies need to be reconciled. Why are we shown the number of Argo profiles in the 3-5N/S bands, if
they are (rightly) not analyzed? It is also not very clear in the body of the text how the density overturns relate to the shear
driven mixing. This is explained in the extended data, but should be mentioned concisely in the main text as well. Related: In
Figure 3 we are looking at the response of mixing indicators to wind stress, which is again not entirely clear to me why. It
needs to be better explained in the text how this relates to shear driven turbulence.
The discussion about the Central Pacific (CP) and Eastern Pacific (EP) is at times not clear. In the abstract it is said that the
CP exhibits a stronger signal, what is meant? Historically EP ENSOs are stronger than CP ENSOs. Do the authors mean
that CP is more frequent in the past two decades? Further, the authors speak about CP and EP but do not show coincidence
of mixing during EP or CP events, just the regions. Side note / related minor comment: in some figures it says that CP and
EP regions are marked, but I cannot see the marking, e.g. in Figure 2b.
The text relies at times heavily on the extended data and figures. Especially the part lines 181 - 216. This makes me wonder
whether this manuscript is suited for a short format publication such as the one the authors have chosen to submit to. In this
section I am also confused about the CP and EP references. The authors do not separate CP from EP Ninos but rather just
the locations over the entire time period. What is the sensitivity of this analysis if it is separated into times of EP and CP
Ninos, and La Nina vs El Nino? Only part of the analysis is split into El Nino and La Nina periods.
General minor remarks (which are personal suggestions that I believe would increase the readability of the work):
For the figure captions please do not say “same as fig x” if the figure is a different one. It is hard to have to go back and forth
between figures to find out what we’re looking at.
DWC is not a good acronym in my opinion. It would be better to actually name the process since it’s so crucial to this work
and diabatic cooling / warming has both sides, so the acronym sounds kind of weird to me.
Minor comments:
Ll 51ff do the authors mean the recharge-discharge mechanism?
L57 the references are too old, there are more modern studies looking at diabatic processes and how they contribute to El
Nino and La Nina variability
L 71 the reference to Fig 1a is not very helpful here, the figure just shows the one point where data is available, not the
difficulties in sampling.
L 88 again 5S-5N is mentioned while in the extended data it is stated that the calculations of mixing events are only done
3S-3N, this needs to be consistent.
L90 “rapidly diminishes” I think this is an overstatement. It pretty much linearly decreases from the maximum.
L 93 the reference to barrier layer mixing events either needs to be explained better or not necessary. This speaks to the
overall a bit “loose” referencing to mixing in this manuscript, this analysis per definition of the method only analysis shear
driven mixing, how is this related to the barrier layer mixing events? Related to the “loose” references: How can the shear
driven mixing be present at say 4S where there is no strong vertical current shear? The reader needs to be explained what
type of mixing we are looking at and why it can arguably be assumed to be active in the region of the study.
L 95 wind forcing and shear instability might induce different types (at different depths) of mixing. Is deep cycle turbulence
distinguished from wind driven turbulence in the upper ocean boundary layer? Are both meant? Is the effect of wind on DCT
meant? More precise language would help the reader.
L 95 - 106 I don’t think I fully follow why this discussion is here. Can you please explain?
L 111-114 instead of just comparing the strength of the shear Ri should be shown to support this argument. Arguably Ri is
hard to estimate from mean fields.
L 115 The explanation of the mixing detection comes too late in the manuscript in my opinion.
Fig 2e CP and EP regions should be indicated
L187-190 should cite references for the intensification of the EUC during La Nina
Fig 3 shows the occurrence of mixing in 5degree latitude blocks though we have established that the analysis only (at most)
works in 3S-3N. What is the sensitivity of the result to reducing the meridional extent? Additionally: why is only the CP
region shown?
Fig 4 a I don’t know if I find this figure outstanding, I find the interannual variability quite hard to see. It might help to add an
indicator of SST anomaly in Nino3.4 or similar to the figure. Over which area are the heat fluxes calculated? Fig 4 now
analysis El Nino and La Nina separately, which is nice. I still think that an addition of occurring EP vs CP Ninos is
necessary. What if the cooling effect in the east actually represses the before dominant EP Ninos?
Data and Method section
Why are GHRSST data used for SST and not ERA5 to be consistent?
L 470 what is the sorted density?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear Reviewer:
Thank you very much for further thinking this issue. It is a good suggestion to distinct the role
of wind stress from the role of strong shear/MI in forming the turbulent mixing around the mixed
layer base. We here try our best to answer your question in the following 3 subsections, which are
followed by the revision to the text according to your suggestion.
1, Two mechanisms for wind stress in promoting the generation of turbulent mixing around the
mixed layer base:
1) Mechanism I: providing a background shear instability condition. The westward zonal wind
stress (of the trade wind) maintains the westward south equatorial current (SEC) in the near-
surface layer via momentum input and the eastward equatorial undercurrent (EUC) in the
subsurface layer via west-east pressure (Yu and Mcphaden, 1999), which jointly form a
background vertical shear above the EUC core. The shear of (primarily) SEC (and possibly also
EUC) beneath the mixed layer base provides the basic precondition for shear instability (random
vorticity and/or internal wave perturbations then may initiate the turbulence). In general, the
stronger the trade wind stress, the stronger equatorial currents and the resulted vertical shear,
and the higher the possibility of turbulence generation. Therefore, it is obviously seen that the
variations of zonal wind stress at longer (>monthly) time scales lead to the variations of both
the shear (Supplementary Fig. 5abcd) and the mixing indicator (Fig. 2d, 3cf, 4bf) at the same
time scales. This mechanism was explained in the Line 230-243 in the last version.
2) Mechanism II: wind-driven entrainment. The wind stress provides momentum input to the
mixed layer, breaks the equilibrium of the ML and leads to entrainment at the mixed layer
bottom, as well shown in both laboratory experiments (e.g., Strang and Fernando 2001) and
direct numerical simulation (DNS) studies (e.g., Pham and Sharkar, 2017). Entrainment is
featured as a process of wind-driven turbulence originated at the mixed layer bottom deepening
the mixed layer into the depths of the original stratified shear flow.
2, Two mechanisms for strong shear/MI in the generation of turbulent mixing beneath the mixed
layer base.
1) Strong shear or MI or low Ri below the mixed layer base favors the occurrence of shear
instability and turbulence, which may be initiated by suitable perturbations from any
mechanisms.
2) This condition also favors the entrainment to develop and to penetrate to a deeper layer, forming
the observed DCL in the central-to-eastern equatorial Pacific.
3, Interwind roles of them under MI conditions, and separated roles in specific conditions
1) It should be clarified that the roles of wind stress and shear are not independent, particularly
under the MI condition which is frequently fulfilled in the central equatorial Pacific (Moum et
al., 2023). This is what our study involves, it is also what many previous works was focusing
on. On the one hand, wind stress controls the strength of shear, which may easily move a
marginal instability condition to a stability or instability condition; on the other hand, strong
shear favors the wind-induced entrainment to develop into DC turbulence, and favors the
entrainment-associated internal wave into shear instability to occur as well, and vice versa. As
such, the MI provides the precondition for the occurrence of turbulence, while the wind stress
initiates the turbulence there– via providing additional shear, its induced internal wave and/or
entrainment at the mixed layer bottom. Moum et al. (2023) observed that stronger wind stress
will lead to larger and quicker enhancement of mixing beneath the mixed layer base. This is the
reason why the proposed parameterization for mixing coefficients constitutes both wind stress
and shear.
2) In contrast, imagine two scenarios where the wind stress and the MI condition are separated
from each other. One is a strong thermocline with weak shear or large Ri just beneath the mixed
layer base, where additional wind stress may lead to entrainment that will be confined in a very
thin layer and can’t support a DC turbulence. If this is the case in the study area, the entrainment-
associated turbulence patch might be very small and can’t be detected by Argo profile data. The
other is a low Ri/MI condition far away from the surface layer, like the observed upper core
layer (UCL, Moum et al., 2009; Inoue et al., 2012), where the shear instability and turbulence
is found by ourselves generated by local dynamics and has nothing to do with wind stress (Liu
et al., 2020). If this is the case in the study area, it is excluded because we focus only on mixing
around the mixed layer base.
4, For the revision of the text:
We revise this section by providing the individual mechanisms of them to distinct their roles in the
generation of EL mixing. We also discuss the complicated interactions between wind- and shear-
induced mixing by providing an additional paragraph.
We modify the wind stress’s role with a long sentence:
“Firstly, wind stress forcing offers one of the basic interpretations for occurrence
of EL mixing. Stronger zonal wind stress (stronger trade wind) leads to higher
occurrence of EL mixing via two mechanisms. The first is it provides stronger vertical
shear and hence more shear instability condition in subsurface layer, which will be
demonstrated in the following subsection, and the second is it leads to stronger and
quicker enhancement of entrainment turbulence, which are demonstrated by laboratory
experiment (Strang and Fernando 2001), direct numerical simulations (Pham and Sharkar,
2017), and observed by several years of turbulence measurements (Moum et al., 2023).”
Similarly, we modify the shear’s role with a longer sentence:
“Secondly, local background shear stability condition20 offers another basic
interpretation for occurrence of EL mixing. The occurrence of EL mixing reflects
fulfillment of local shear instability therein.”
Moreover, we also added a paragraph below those two paragraphs to clarify their combined roles:
“It is noted that the roles of wind stress and shear in promoting the generation of
EL mixing are not independent, particularly under the MI condition which is frequently
fulfilled in the central-to-eastern equatorial Pacific region (170°E–110°W). On the one
hand, wind stress controls the strength of subsurface background shear and the
initiation of entrainment at the MLB, on the other hand, strong background shear or
MI favors shear instability and the wind-driven entrainment to develop into deep cycle
turbulence. Overall, the MI in the subsurface layer provides the precondition for the
occurrence of turbulence, while the wind stress initiates the turbulence there.”
We hope we have addressed your concern and made the manuscript clearer. Thank you again.

strongly sheared turbulent layer in the eastern equatorial Pacific: Interplays of multiple-time-scale

The manuscript “Subsurface Ocean Turbulent Mixing Enhances Central Pacific ENSO as Positive Feedback” by Liu et al
demonstrates the impact of vertical turbulent mixing on sea surface temperature variability in the equatorial Pacific. The

authors also assert that there is a more pronounced effect of the mixing feedback on Central Pacific ENSO events (CP)

strong current shear is shown in for example Johnson et al (2002) or Roger (Karnasukas et al 2020) to span at most 2S-2N.

shear is not necessarily needed; what it really depends on is the relative intensity of the
shear with respect to the stratification. In other words, if the shear is moderate and the

Secondly, the MI condition needs not be hold all the time - when this condition is
fulfilled (maybe occasionally and in a short period), it provides likelihood for
turbulence to occur, in contrast, when it is not fulfilled, turbulence would less likely to

overturns. Once turbulence occurs, it is assumed the MI condition is met. This could be

disappears.
Regarding the MI in the off-equatorial region, we know that the westward flowing

shear at the MLB and EL depths. Though the shear in 2°S-2°N region is strengthened

meanwhile, the other factor that needs to be considered is the strength of stratification
near the MLB. Also from Johnson’s observations, we see that the stratification is weak
around the MLB, providing the possibility to form MI condition. The SEC shear could
be strengthened or weakened by the zonal wind, which results in higher or lower
likelihood of MI and turbulence in the ELs. We show the Ri along 3 meridional sections

the CP region and weak (insignificant) eastward zonal anomaly in the EP region,
resembling that of a typical CP type La Nina. Therefore, the present analysis on “CP
region” can be regarded as that on a “CP type”.

eastern part, so that we can’t call the diabatic effect as a positive feedback mechanism
